data.title: OAuth
data.tagline: A protocol for granting a client scoped access to protected resources
data.learningOutcome: You can distinguish OAuth resource authorization from the identity verification needed for third-party sign-in.
data.description: After a user approves, an OAuth access token lets a client access a protected resource within its granted scope; the token itself is not generic proof of identity. A site using a provider account for sign-in commonly also needs OpenID Connect or the provider's explicit identity mechanism, then maps that identity to its own user.

learning.assumes: You have seen sign in with WeChat / Google buttons, or used third-party sign-in yourself.
learning.outcome: You can distinguish OAuth resource authorization from the identity verification needed for third-party sign-in.

distinctions.label: Authentication
distinctions.explanation: Authentication confirms a user's identity; OAuth authorizes a client to access resources and does not by itself define a generic sign-in identity. Third-party sign-in commonly uses OpenID Connect or a provider identity mechanism.

distinctions.label: Password sign-in
distinctions.explanation: Self-registration makes users remember a new password; OAuth can authorize a client to access a resource, but authorization alone does not establish the user's identity.

explanation.title: Jump to the third party to confirm
explanation.text: Clicking sign in with WeChat jumps to WeChat's authorization page; the user approves on a platform they know.

explanation.title: Return with the result
explanation.text: After approval you return to the site with an authorization result; the whole flow never touches the user's WeChat password.

explanation.title: The site still identifies the user
explanation.text: The site uses its own user records to recognize who this is; OAuth grants resource access; it is not authentication and does not replace the site's account system.

data.boundary: OAuth is not a sign-in identity protocol. For provider sign-in, confirm the provider identity mechanism and map it to the site user; provide another sign-in path if the product requires it when authorization is revoked or the provider is unavailable.

lessonPractice.title: The product wants third-party sign-in but will keep email registration. What should be confirmed first?

options.label: Confirm the provider identity mechanism as well as authorization, then map that identity to the site user
options.feedback: Correct. OAuth authorization alone does not prove who the user is; sign-in also needs provider identity verification and a mapping to the site user. Email registration can coexist.

options.label: Once OAuth is added, no account system is needed at all
options.feedback: The site still needs its own user records to identify who is who; OAuth only handles the authorization confirmation step.

options.label: The user tells the site their WeChat password to sign in
options.feedback: The point of OAuth is that the site never touches third-party passwords; after authorization it only gets the result.

data.agentPrompt: Add a third-party sign-in option. First confirm whether the provider uses OpenID Connect or its official identity API; configure the authorization callback, verify the identity, and then match or create a site user. Keep email registration unchanged and explain how to verify successful sign-in and failure messages.
